questions.prompt: What makes focus the first OKR superpower in this chapter?
choices: It helps teams choose what matters most instead of keeping every worthy goal active
It proves that smaller goals are always better than bigger ones
It removes the need for stakeholder buy-in

explanation.gentle: The chapter presents focus as hard selection, not as generic reduction.
explanation.direct: Focus matters because it tells the team what truly leads and what no longer does.
explanation.competitive: The superpower starts when worthy alternatives start losing.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter distinguish commitment from awareness?
choices: Awareness is enough if the goal sounds important
Commitment means participation and buy-in that change behavior
Commitment means forcing compliance without discussion

explanation.gentle: Hearing the goal is not the same as carrying it.
explanation.direct: The chapter defines commitment through buy-in and changed effort allocation.
explanation.competitive: A repeated slogan is not a commitment. A reorganized week is.

questions.prompt: Why do too many priorities weaken execution according to the chapter?
choices: Because teams lose the ability to guide action around what matters most
Because worthy goals are usually incorrect
Because fewer priorities always mean lower ambition

explanation.gentle: The problem is overload, not ambition itself.
explanation.direct: Too many active priorities borrow force from one another until the system turns noisy.
explanation.competitive: If everything wants first place, nothing really leads.

questions.prompt: Sonia roadmap still has six items marked top priority. What move best fits the chapter?
choices: Keep all six to avoid disappointing sponsors
Cut the list to the few items that can truly lead this quarter
Add two more so the roadmap feels balanced

explanation.gentle: The chapter would force a smaller real priority stack.
explanation.direct: Focus requires visible sacrifice, not a broader top tier.
explanation.competitive: A roadmap with six leaders is hiding the lack of a leader.

questions.prompt: Claire capstone team kept every workstream active until deadline week. What chapter failure does this show?
choices: A healthy version of broad ambition
Overload created by failing to rank worthy goals
Too much commitment to the chosen priorities

explanation.gentle: The postmortem problem is not laziness. It is weak selection.
explanation.direct: The chapter treats overload as the failure mode where every worthy stream keeps asking to lead.
explanation.competitive: Hard work cannot rescue a team that never ranked the work honestly.

questions.prompt: Why is it a weak reading to say commitment means compliance alone?
choices: Because the chapter ignores behavior entirely
Because the chapter defines commitment as earned participation and buy-in, not just obedience
Because compliance always produces stronger focus

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps commitment tied to participation and real carry, not passive submission.
explanation.direct: Buy-in matters because the chosen goal must govern behavior, not just language.
explanation.competitive: Forced agreement can clean up the meeting without changing the work.

questions.prompt: A team keeps every worthy idea alive because nobody wants to disappoint stakeholders. What does the chapter say is happening?
choices: The team is protecting ambition in the best possible way
The team is preserving overload and weakening execution
The team has already shown strong commitment

explanation.gentle: The chapter says worthiness is not enough. Priority requires ranking and loss.
explanation.direct: Keeping every good idea active usually means overload has survived the planning meeting.
explanation.competitive: When no worthy option loses, the system stays soft and noisy.

questions.prompt: Devin team agreed with a new objective, but calendars and sprint lines still protect the old work. Which judgment fits the chapter best?
choices: The team has symbolic alignment instead of real commitment
The team is wisely avoiding sacrifice
The team has too much focus already

explanation.gentle: The chapter separates public agreement from behavioral buy-in.
explanation.direct: If the old work still owns the week, the new commitment is mostly language.
explanation.competitive: A nodding room can still be a hedging room.

questions.prompt: What severe truth about focus does the chapter keep alive?
choices: Focus works only when leaders are willing to disappoint attractive alternatives
Focus means reducing ambition until nobody feels pressure
Focus removes the need to explain tradeoffs to stakeholders

explanation.gentle: Sacrifice is built into focus. That is part of the discipline.
explanation.direct: The chapter refuses the fantasy of priority without exclusion.
explanation.competitive: If nothing attractive loses, focus is still cosmetic.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 4 naturally lead into a company story next?
choices: Because the book now wants to leave operating logic behind
Because the reader should now see what focus and commitment look like inside a real case
Because general principles are no longer relevant after this chapter

explanation.gentle: The bridge asks what this superpower looks like once a company has to live inside it.
explanation.direct: After the rule layer, the next useful move is a concrete company story.
explanation.competitive: Theory has set the standard. The next chapter has to make it real.
